title: Fragile X and Rett syndromes
blurb: Recognise fragile X and Rett syndromes, explain their X-linked genetics, and adjust nursing care to their anxiety, seizure, breathing and postural needs.
question: Hana, 4, has Rett syndrome and is admitted for dental treatment under general anaesthetic. While awake she holds her breath for several seconds and then breathes rapidly. Her mother says this happens every day. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Fragile X syndrome and Rett syndrome both arise from genes on the X chromosome, but they look very different. Fragile X is caused by changes in the FMR1 gene; boys are usually more severely affected. Rett syndrome is caused by changes in the MECP2 gene and is seen almost entirely in girls, who lose skills after a period of apparently normal development. In plain English: same chromosome, different gene, different story.

rows.label: Hallmark
values: Loss of hand use, hand wringing

teach.caption: A premutation carrier usually has no learning disability but can pass on a repeat that expands to a full mutation.

teach.h: Why boys are usually more affected
teach.body: Males have one X chromosome. If their FMR1 gene carries a full mutation, they have no working copy. Females have two X chromosomes, and the second usually carries a working copy, so effects are often milder. Most males with fragile X have a mild to moderate learning disability; about one third of affected females have a learning disability. Because carriers may be well, relatives should be offered genetic counselling.

teach.h: Fragile X: features to plan for
teach.caption: Physical features can include a long narrow face, large ears, prominent jaw and forehead and very flexible fingers.

teach.h: Nursing a person with fragile X
teach.body: Social anxiety and gaze aversion are common: looking away is not rudeness or inattention. Reduce waiting and noise (first or last appointment, a quiet space), give clear warning of what will happen, and let the person avoid eye contact while talking. Watch for seizures. Many have autistic features and may need sensory adjustments.

items.label: Loses purposeful hand use and speech

teach.caption: Also: slowed head and body growth, sleep problems, cold hands and feet. More than 99% have no family history.

teach.h: Nursing a person with Rett syndrome
teach.body: Breathing irregularities while awake (breath-holding, rapid breathing) are part of the condition: know the person's usual pattern, but never let that stop a full assessment when she is unwell. Seizures need a care plan. Scoliosis needs postural care and monitoring. Feeding difficulties and slow growth need dietetic and speech and language therapy input. Without purposeful hand use, people often communicate with their eyes, so offer eye-gaze choices.

Hana's breath-holding followed by rapid breathing while awake matches the breathing irregularities of Rett syndrome, and her mother confirms it is her daily pattern. The nurse records the pattern and its usual length in her notes, tells the anaesthetist, and still completes full observations including oxygen saturation. If an episode is longer, she looks different, or she has a seizure, the nurse escalates. Knowing the baseline prevents both panic and complacency.

teach.text: Rett vs autism: both can show withdrawal and loss of babble in a toddler, but LOSS OF PURPOSEFUL HAND USE with hand wringing points to Rett. And don't swap the genes: Rett = MECP2; fragile X = FMR1 (CGG repeats).

items: Fragile X: FMR1, over 200 CGG repeats; premutation 55–200; males usually more affected.
Fragile X: anxiety, gaze aversion, autistic features (~1 in 3), seizures; offer counselling to relatives.
Rett: MECP2, almost all girls, over 99% new; 6–18 months normal then regression.
Rett: hand wringing, loss of speech, breathing irregularities, seizures, scoliosis.
Know the baseline, but assess fully when unwell.

summary: You can now explain the X-linked genetics of fragile X and Rett syndromes, recognise their key features, and adapt care: reducing anxiety and accepting gaze aversion in fragile X, and managing breathing, seizure, postural and feeding needs in Rett syndrome.

A.q: A student asks which developmental pattern is typical of classic Rett syndrome. Which is correct?
options: Low muscle tone and poor feeding from birth, then overeating
6 to 18 months of apparently normal development, then regression
Typical development until about five years, then gradual decline
Slow steady development from birth with no loss of skills
A.why: Girls with classic Rett syndrome have 6 to 18 months of apparently normal development, then lose purposeful hand use and speech.

whyNot.0: This is the pattern in Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyNot.2: Regression in Rett starts much earlier, in the second year of life.
whyNot.3: Loss of skills (regression) is the defining feature of Rett.

A.q: About what proportion of people with fragile X syndrome have features of autism?
options: About one in twenty
About two thirds
Almost everyone
About one third
A.why: MedlinePlus Genetics: about one third of individuals with fragile X syndrome have features of autism.

whyNot.2: Autistic features are common but not universal.

A.q: A student asks why Rett syndrome is seen almost entirely in girls. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The MECP2 gene sits on the Y chromosome
Girls inherit the gene change from their fathers
Boys are protected by their second X chromosome
Males with MECP2 mutations often die in infancy
A.why: Rett is X-linked dominant. Males with MECP2 mutations often die in infancy, so the syndrome is seen almost entirely in girls.

whyNot.0: MECP2 is on the X chromosome.
whyNot.1: More than 99% of cases are new mutations, not inherited.
whyNot.2: Boys have one X chromosome, not two.

B.q: Kayden, 9, has fragile X syndrome. His teacher reports brief episodes where he stares blankly and does not respond for a few seconds, several times a day. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report them for medical assessment of possible seizures
Record them as daydreaming linked to his attention difficulties
Add more sensory breaks to his school timetable
Use an ABC chart to find what triggers the staring
B.why: Seizures occur in about 15% of males with fragile X. Brief unresponsive staring episodes need medical assessment.

whyNot.1: Attributing them to attention difficulties risks missing epilepsy.
whyNot.2: Sensory breaks do not address possible seizures.
whyNot.3: Behaviour analysis would delay medical assessment.

B.q: Aisha, 7, has a full fragile X mutation. Her parents ask what this usually means for girls. Which statement is accurate?
options: Girls with a full mutation are unaffected carriers
Girls are usually more severely affected than boys
About one third of affected girls have a learning disability
Girls with a full mutation usually have a severe learning disability
B.why: Females have a second X that usually carries a working FMR1 copy; about one third of affected females have a learning disability.

whyNot.0: A full mutation can affect girls, though often more mildly than boys.
whyNot.1: Boys are usually more severely affected.
whyNot.3: Most affected girls do not have a severe learning disability.

B.q: Hana, 4, has Rett syndrome and is waiting for dental treatment. While awake she holds her breath, then breathes rapidly. Her mother says this happens every day and Hana looks her usual self. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Put out an emergency call while the episode is happening
Give oxygen continuously until the episodes have stopped
Record her usual pattern and still complete full observations
Ask her mother to stop the episodes using distraction
B.why: Breathing irregularities while awake are part of Rett syndrome. Recording her baseline and telling the anaesthetist helps, but full observations are still needed to spot real deterioration.

whyNot.0: Her usual pattern, with her looking well, is not an emergency.
whyNot.1: Continuous oxygen is not indicated for her usual breathing pattern.
whyNot.3: These episodes are part of the condition, not behaviour to distract away.

C.q: Ahmed, 24, has a moderate learning disability, a long narrow face, large ears, very flexible fingers and marked social anxiety. His mother says her brother had similar difficulties. Which syndrome is most likely?
options: Down syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Angelman syndrome
C.why: These physical features with anxiety, a learning disability and an affected maternal uncle fit fragile X, an X-linked condition passed through the maternal line.

whyNot.0: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 and is not usually inherited through a maternal uncle pattern.
whyNot.2: Prader-Willi is marked by hyperphagia and short stature.
whyNot.3: Angelman causes severe learning disability, minimal speech and frequent laughter.

C.q: During an assessment, Ahmed, who has fragile X syndrome, looks away whenever the nurse asks a question but answers accurately. A colleague says he is 'not engaging'. What is the best response?
options: Gaze aversion is common in fragile X; let him look away as he talks
Ask him to look at you so you can be sure he understands
Record in his notes that he is not engaging with the assessment
Ask his mother to answer the questions on his behalf instead
C.why: Social anxiety and gaze aversion are common in fragile X. Ahmed is engaging and answering accurately; allowing him to look away reduces anxiety.

whyNot.1: Insisting on eye contact increases his anxiety and is not needed to show understanding.
whyNot.2: This would be inaccurate; he is answering accurately.
whyNot.3: He can answer for himself; speaking for him undermines his rights.

C.q: Grace, 15, has Rett syndrome. Over six months meals have taken longer, she has lost weight and she has had two chest infections. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Offer larger portions at each meal to restore her weight
Record the change as part of the expected course of Rett
Refer for swallowing and nutrition assessment
Start a behaviour plan to address food refusal
C.why: Longer meals, weight loss and chest infections suggest unsafe swallowing and poor nutrition, which need speech and language therapy and dietetic assessment.

whyNot.0: Bigger portions do not address possible aspiration.
whyNot.1: Treatable problems should not be accepted as 'part of Rett'; that is diagnostic overshadowing.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests refusal; these are signs of a swallowing problem.

reteach.title: Same chromosome, two stories
reteach.question: If both syndromes come from the X chromosome, how do you tell them apart in practice?

blocks.body: Who? Fragile X affects boys more severely; Rett is almost always girls. When? Fragile X shows as delay from early childhood; Rett follows apparently normal development with regression at 6 to 18 months. What stands out? Anxiety, gaze aversion and autistic features in fragile X; loss of hand use with hand wringing in Rett.

blocks.text: CGG repeats belong to fragile X. Over 200 = full mutation; 55 to 200 = premutation carrier.

explain.body: Typical: about 5 to 40 repeats. Premutation: 55 to 200 (carrier, can pass it on). Full mutation: over 200, which silences the gene and causes fragile X.

test.q: A genetic report shows 120 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene of a woman with no learning disability. What does this mean?
options: She has a full mutation
She is a premutation carrier
She has a typical repeat number
She has Rett syndrome
test.why: 55 to 200 repeats is a premutation: usually no learning disability, but it can expand to a full mutation in her children.

whyNot.0: A full mutation is over 200 repeats.
whyNot.3: Rett is caused by MECP2, not FMR1 repeats.

explain.body: Mild to moderate learning disability in most males; about one third of females. Anxiety, hyperactivity, autistic features in about one third, seizures in about 15% of males and 5% of females.

test.q: Which reasonable adjustment best suits an anxious teenager with fragile X attending a busy clinic?
options: A quiet place to wait and the first appointment of the day
A longer wait so he can get used to the busy room
A request that he keeps eye contact during the consultation
A group session with other patients to build confidence
test.why: Reducing waiting and sensory load eases the anxiety common in fragile X.

whyNot.1: Longer waits in a busy room increase anxiety.
whyNot.2: Gaze aversion is common; insisting on eye contact raises anxiety.
whyNot.3: A group setting increases social demand.

explain.body: 6 to 18 months of apparently normal development, then regression: loss of purposeful hand use and speech, with repetitive hand wringing, washing or clapping. Over 99% are new mutations.

test.q: Which finding most points to Rett syndrome rather than autism in a toddler who has stopped babbling?
options: Lining up toys in long straight rows
Loss of hand use with hand wringing
Marked distress at changes in routine
Limited eye contact with her parents
test.why: Loss of purposeful hand use replaced by hand wringing is the hallmark of Rett and is not a feature of autism.

whyNot.0: Lining up objects is more typical of autism.
whyNot.2: Distress at change is common in autism.
whyNot.3: Limited eye contact occurs in both and does not distinguish them.

explain.body: Breathing irregularities while awake, seizures, scoliosis, slow growth and feeding problems, sleep disturbance. Monitor posture and spine, plan for seizures, and involve dietetics and speech and language therapy.

test.q: Nia, 11, has Rett syndrome and attends her annual review with the community nurse. Which complication linked to her syndrome should be checked?
options: Curvature of the spine
Excessive hunger
Early-onset dementia
Underactive thyroid
test.why: Scoliosis is a recognised feature of Rett syndrome and needs regular monitoring and postural care.

whyNot.1: Hyperphagia is a feature of Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyNot.2: Early-onset Alzheimer's is linked to Down syndrome.
whyNot.3: Hypothyroidism is linked to Down syndrome.
